::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The end-of-course project goal

Your team answers a predictive question with a public data set, in R and/or Python,
with a focus on reproducible and trustworthy workflows.
**By the end of the course**, your single Quarto document will have become a project with:

-   well-documented, modular scripts in R and/or Python
-   a pipeline automated with GNU Make
-   a reproducible Quarto report
-   a Docker container for the computational environment
-   a GitHub repository for collaboration and sharing
:::

::: callout-important
## Find your group

Check that you are in the right group, with the right teammates, in the
[lab sections file](https://github.ubc.ca/mds-2026-27/lab-sections/blob/main/lab_section_block3_2026-27.csv).
:::

## Milestone 1 summary

This milestone is about doing **a complete data analysis project from start to finish**:
read in the raw data, clean it, fit a model, get results, and write them up in a professional report.
The analysis can be simple, but **the report must be detailed, accurate and professional**.
You don't need Docker, scripts or Make yet: that comes in later milestones.

- [ ] Write a teamwork contract
- [ ] Set up a public GitHub repository in the course organization, **with its [metadata]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="Metadata is data about data: information that describes something, not the thing itself (a photo's date and location, a book's author and title). Here it means the information that describes your GitHub repository, not your code: where it lives (the course organization), its Description (starting with DSCI 522), and which teams can access it. The teaching team's grading scripts use it to find your repository."}**
- [ ] Give it a tidy project structure and the standard project files
- [ ] Do the full analysis and write the report in one Quarto document (`.qmd`)
- [ ] Record your environment with uv (Python) or renv (R), **as you go, not at the end**

::: callout-note
## You only lose points once for the same mistake

If you lose points for something in one milestone, we won't take points off again for it in later milestones.
Still fix it: later milestones build on this work, and in Milestone 4 you can win back some of those points.
:::

Your reference is the example project at the end of Milestone 1:
[Breast Cancer Predictor 0.0.1](https://github.com/UBC-MDS/DSCI_522_project-template-breast-cancer-predictor/tree/0.0.1).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

### 1. Write a teamwork contract

Copy the [teamwork contract template](teamwork-contract.qmd) into a Quarto document,
make it your team's own, and render it to PDF.
**Talk it through as a team**: a rushed contract, or one left mostly as the template, loses marks.
It is personal, so it goes to Gradescope, not into your public repository.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What a contract usually covers

-   How you share the work fairly
-   Expected work hours, and when each of you is not available
-   How often you meet, and who writes agendas and minutes
-   How you work day to day (e.g., [stand-ups](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/scrum/standups), or a written update before each meeting)
-   The quality of work you expect from yourselves and each other
-   How you will handle conflict
:::

### 2. Set up your GitHub repository

Create a **public** repository for your group in the
[UBC-MDS-2026-27](https://github.com/orgs/UBC-MDS-2026-27) organization
(not under a personal account or `UBC-MDS`).
Give it a name related to your question; you can rename it later.
All your project work lives in this repository.

::: callout-important
## Repository metadata is graded, and the course automation relies on it

[Metadata]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="Metadata is data about data: information that describes something, not the thing itself (a photo's date and location, a book's author and title). Here it means the information that describes your GitHub repository, not your code: where it lives (the course organization), its Description (starting with DSCI 522), and which teams can access it. The teaching team's grading scripts use it to find your repository."} that is wrong at the Milestone 1 deadline loses points in Milestone 1 only.
Please still fix it: the course automation needs it.
Check it in your first lab, and raise any problem with the teaching team there.
:::

1.  It lives in [UBC-MDS-2026-27](https://github.com/orgs/UBC-MDS-2026-27).
2.  Its **Description starts with exactly `DSCI 522`** (capital `DSCI`, one space, `522`, nothing before it),
    e.g. `DSCI 522: Predicting wine quality from its chemistry`.
    Not `dsci 522`, `DSCI522`, `DSCI-522` or `Predicting wine quality (DSCI 522)`.
    Edit it with the gear icon next to **About** on the repository's main page.
3.  It is added to **two teams**: `522-students` with the **Read** role,
    and your group's team `522-team-XX` (your group number as two digits, e.g. `522-team-01`) with the **Admin** role.

**Each team member** checks their own:

1.  You accepted the invitation to the organization

2.  You are listed under **Members** of both `522-students` and your `522-team-XX`

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How to add the teams and check them

1.  Open your repository's **Settings \> Collaborators and teams \> Add teams**.
    You need admin access; whoever created the repository has it.
2.  Search for each team and pick its role (Read for `522-students`, Admin for your group's team).
    Admin for your group's team gives every member admin access, which you need later (e.g. for GitHub secrets in Milestone 2).
3.  Check that your repository is listed under each team's **Repositories** tab:
    -   <https://github.com/orgs/UBC-MDS-2026-27/teams/522-students/repositories>
    -   <https://github.com/orgs/UBC-MDS-2026-27/teams/522-team-01/repositories> (use your group's number)

To find your group's team: in the [organization](https://github.com/orgs/UBC-MDS-2026-27),
open **Teams \> 522-students**; it is listed there as a sub-team.
:::

### 3. Give your project a tidy structure

Your repository should look like this.
Keep only the files that apply to you (the uv files for Python, the renv files for R, or both).

```
your-project-name/
├── README.md
├── CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
├── CONTRIBUTING.md
├── LICENSE.md
├── .gitignore              # at least .DS_Store and .venv/
├── pyproject.toml          # Python (uv)
├── uv.lock                 # Python (uv)
├── .python-version         # Python (uv)
├── renv.lock               # R (renv)
├── .Rprofile               # R (renv)
├── renv/                   # R (renv): follow the .gitignore in here
├── data/
│   ├── raw/                # data exactly as downloaded
│   └── processed/          # cleaned / intermediate data
└── analysis/               # or reports/, src/
    ├── <descriptive-name>.qmd
    └── <descriptive-name>.html  # or .pdf
```

Keep the root tidy: the report goes in a sub-folder, not the root.

What each file needs:

-   **`README.md`**: the project title; all authors; a short summary (your question, what you found, what it might mean);
    **step-by-step instructions to run the analysis**, from cloning to rendering the report;
    the dependencies (or a link to `pyproject.toml`); the license names;
    an AI use statement; and a link to the rendered report.
-   **`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`**: a statement on diversity and inclusion, expected and unacceptable behaviour,
    consequences, and how to report problems.
-   **`CONTRIBUTING.md`**: how someone outside your team reports a bug, suggests a change and submits work,
    **plus an AI policy section** for contributors.
-   **`LICENSE.md`**: **two licenses**, one for the code (e.g. [MIT](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))
    and one for the report (e.g. [CC BY-NC-ND 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/)),
    with the full license text pasted in and all team members in the copyright line.
    Name it exactly `LICENSE.md`, and make the README name the same licenses.
-   **`data/`**: written by code in your report (not downloaded by hand),
    raw data in `data/raw/`, everything you make from it in `data/processed/`.
    If a file is over 100 MB, ask the teaching team for another plan and explain it in your README.
-   **`analysis/<descriptive-name>.qmd`**: your one report, with a descriptive name (not `analysis.qmd`).
    Push it **and** its rendered HTML or PDF. Delete drafts and scratch files.
-   **Environment files**: see [section 5](#make-the-computational-environment-reproducible).

If you adapt a code of conduct, contributing guide or AI policy, **cite the original** (name and link),
replace its contact email with your team's, and leave no template placeholders.
Click every link in these files and proofread them.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## More on the README AI use statement

Say whether you used generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot) and, if so, how, with a few example prompts.
If you used instruction files (e.g., `CLAUDE.md`), commit them and point to them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

-   **Codes of conduct:** [Project Include guide](https://projectinclude.org/writing_cocs),
    [Python](https://www.python.org/psf/conduct/),
    [Tidyverse](https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyverse.org/blob/master/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md),
    [pandas](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas-governance/blob/master/code-of-conduct.md)
-   **Contributing guides:** [Altair](https://github.com/altair-viz/altair/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md),
    [dplyr](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/master/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md),
    [AI fairness research paper](https://github.com/skysheng7/AI_bias_in_farming/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
-   **AI policies:** [earthaccess](https://earthaccess.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contributor/ai-policy/),
    [SciPy](https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/dev/conduct/ai_policy.html),
    [SymPy](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/contributing/ai-generated-code-policy.html).
    Yours must match the course rule: people, not AI agents, open, review and merge pull requests and issues.
-   **Choosing licenses:** <https://choosealicense.com/>, <https://chooser-beta.creativecommons.org/>.
    You can change your licenses later, once we cover them in the course.
:::

### 4. Do the full analysis and write the report {#write-the-data-analysis}

Answer a predictive question with a model you have already learned in MDS,
in **one `.qmd`** with Python or R code, written like a short scientific report.
It must cover the whole project: raw data in, cleaning, model, results, conclusions.
Use a **public, openly licensed** data set.

::: callout-important
## Keep the analysis simple, make the report excellent

-   **A simple model is fine**, for example one linear regression.
    Machine learning is not the focus of this course, so a fancier model earns no extra marks.
-   **Breaking the golden rule of machine learning loses points**:
    split off the test set before you explore or preprocess the data,
    and don't let it influence any decision.
-   **The report is where the marks are.** It should be detailed, accurate and professional:
    every claim matches your figures and tables, and a reader new to the topic can follow it.
:::
Avoid data that needs a login (e.g. Kaggle); if you use one, your README must walk through getting and setting up the API token.

Your report needs these sections:

-   **Title**
-   **Summary**: one paragraph with your question, what you found, why it matters and the main limitations.
-   **Introduction**: background, why the question matters, the question itself,
    the data set (source, what a row is, the variables you use, with a citation) and your target variable.
-   **Methods**: what you did and why, the model and the metric you chose and why, and code that:
    -   downloads the data from its source into `data/raw/`
    -   cleans it and saves it to `data/processed/`
    -   splits it into training and test sets **before** any exploration or preprocessing (the golden rule: the test set influences no decision)
    -   summarizes and visualizes the training data in a way relevant to your question
    -   fits the classification or regression model
-   **Results**: the figures and tables that answer your question, each numbered, captioned and referred to in the text.
-   **Discussion**: what you found and what it means for the problem, whether you expected it,
    assumptions and limitations, possible impact and future questions.
-   **References**: at least 4, including the data set, each cited in the text.
    Real, reputable sources only (check that AI didn't make them up).

Write in full sentences (point form for at most a few places),
use plain words instead of code names ("flipper length", not `flipper_length_mm`),
spell out acronyms the first time, and proofread. Make sure it renders without errors.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Making figures and tables readable

-   Label axes in plain English, with units.
-   Add a legend when there is more than one colour or group, and use a readable text size.
-   Avoid overplotting (e.g., with transparency).
-   Show only the rows and columns that matter in tables, with clear column names. Don't print a giant data frame.
-   Writing figure and table numbers and captions by hand is fine for now.
-   Check that what you write matches what the figures and tables show.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Where to find a data set

-   [City of Vancouver Open Data Portal](https://opendata.vancouver.ca/pages/home/)
-   [BC Data Catalogue](https://catalogue.data.gov.bc.ca/)
-   [Government of Canada open data](https://open.canada.ca/en/open-data)
-   [Awesome public datasets](https://github.com/awesomedata/awesome-public-datasets)
-   [UCI Machine Learning Repository](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/)
-   [TidyTuesday](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday)
-   [Google Dataset Search](https://toolbox.google.com/datasetsearch)
-   [fivethirtyeight R package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/fivethirtyeight/vignettes/fivethirtyeight.html):
    don't copy the question, figures or methods from the original FiveThirtyEight articles,
    and read the data with `read_*` functions from the
    [raw versions](https://github.com/rudeboybert/fivethirtyeight/tree/master/data-raw).
:::

### 5. Make your environment reproducible {#make-the-computational-environment-reproducible}

Record your packages with **uv** (Python) or **renv** (R) while you write the analysis,
and commit the files shown in the project structure above (never `.venv/`).
See the DSCI 521 notes for [uv](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/virtual-environments-uv.html)
or [renv](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/virtual-environments-renv.html).

::: callout-important
## 5 all-or-nothing points for your README instructions

If someone can't set up your environment and run your analysis by following your README
**exactly as written**, you lose all 5 points.
Test them on **both Windows and Mac**.
If your team doesn't have both, ask another team to test them.
:::

## Submission instructions

1.  Just before you submit, create a GitHub release named exactly `0.0.1`
    ([how to create a release](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/releasing-projects-on-github/managing-releases-in-a-repository#creating-a-release)),
    pointing at your final Milestone 1 work.
    It records the state of your repository at submission, so you can keep working on the next milestone.
2.  On Gradescope, enter these (there is no PDF of links to make):
    -   your project's GitHub.com repository URL
    -   the URL of the `0.0.1` release
    -   your teamwork contract, uploaded as a PDF

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself before submitting

- [ ] The repository is public, in UBC-MDS-2026-27, its Description starts with `DSCI 522`, and it is in both teams
- [ ] Every team member is in the organization and both teams, with their username right in the lab sections file
- [ ] `README.md`, `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` (with an AI policy) and `LICENSE.md` (two licenses) are in the root
- [ ] The report downloads its data into `data/raw/` and splits before exploring
- [ ] The rendered report is pushed next to the `.qmd`, and there is only one report
- [ ] Someone on Windows and someone on Mac followed your README exactly and rendered the report
- [ ] You created the `0.0.1` release
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Teamwork expectations (these are marked)

-   **Everyone contributes equally** to code, writing and project management,
    shown by a roughly equal number of commits, pull request reviews and GitHub issue comments.
-   Use the [GitHub flow](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/quickstart/github-flow) in your team's repository (not a fork):
    one small branch per feature or fix, with a meaningful name (e.g. `add-eda-plot`, not `branch1`),
    and a pull request reviewed by at least one teammate before it is merged. Don't push straight to `main`.
-   Commit and push every time you work on the project, with meaningful commit messages
    (one or two less meaningful ones are OK).
-   Talk to your teammates in GitHub issues, not email or Slack: for planning, splitting tasks and decisions.
    Aim for more than 3 issues per person.
-   You open pull requests and issues yourselves, not an AI agent.
    AI can help check code, but people review and merge.
-   Your question, analysis and visualization should make sense. They don't have to be complicated.
-   Write your README and report in full sentences with proper grammar. Keep point form under 10%.
:::
